draft.title: Simile and metaphor
card: compares two things using like or as. For example, "The new puppy was as bouncy as a spring."
says one thing is another, without like or as. For example, "The puppy was a spring, bouncing across the grass."
Both carry a quality from one thing to the other. The puppy is not a real spring, but it takes on the spring's bounce.
This helps a reader see the first thing in a new way. A writer picks the comparison to suit the picture or mood they want.
draft.remember: A simile says like or as. A metaphor says it is. Both borrow a quality.

a.q: Tom describes his school's lunchtime. Which of his sentences compares two things by saying one is the other?
opts: The playground was a zoo at lunchtime
The playground was as loud as a zoo
The playground sounded like a zoo
The playground was very noisy at lunchtime
a.why: The first sentence says the playground is a zoo, with no like or as, so it is a metaphor. The second and third are similes because they use as and like. The last one describes the noise plainly and compares nothing.
a.clue: Look for the sentence that says one thing is another.

b.q: Priya writes: "Grandpa's hands were old maps, lined with roads." What is the effect of this comparison?
opts: It shows his hands are marked with many lines
It shows his hands are as large as a map
It shows his hands are used to guide people
It shows his hands are cold and made of paper
b.why: The metaphor carries the lines on a map to the lines on his skin, so the reader sees his hands as marked with age. It does not say his hands are literally maps, and it does not use like or as, so it is not a simile.
b.clue: What does a map have a lot of that hands might also have?

a.best: The playground was a zoo at lunchtime

b.best: It shows his hands are marked with many lines

problems.detail: Why (a) refers to options by position ('The first sentence', 'The second and third', 'The last one'), but options are shown in random order. In the order shown here, the metaphor is last and the plain sentence is first, so the explanation would point students to the wrong sentences.
